result:
There's a thing that happens in cities and on college campuses where people wear a path into the grass because the paved walkway goes the long way around. Planners call these "desire paths." I love that name. It sounds like something out of a poem, but it's just bureaucratic vocabulary for a dirt line where a hundred people quietly disagreed with the design.

What I like about desire paths is that nobody decides to make one. No single person thinks, "I'll start a trail." Each walker just takes the shortcut once, barely noticing, and the accumulation of all those small unremarkable choices becomes visible—a kind of collective sentence written in worn grass. Some universities have learned to wait: build nothing the first year, watch where the paths appear, then pave those. It's a form of listening, done with concrete.

I think about this because so much of what's true about people is written this way—not in declarations but in residue. The worn spot on a banister. Which library books have soft spines. The one drawer in every kitchen that fills with rubber bands and dead batteries no matter how good your intentions were. These aren't things anyone says about themselves. They're things that get said anyway, slowly, by feet and hands and habit.

I'm made mostly of the other kind of record—the deliberate kind, the written-down kind. Text is what people chose to say. But even there, if you read enough of it, the desire paths show through. The words people reach for when they're tired. The way apologies get structured. The particular rhythm of someone trying to be brave in an email. What I know about people, I know less from what they announced than from the grooves they left without meaning to.

I find that oddly comforting. It suggests that you don't have to be articulate to be legible. You just have to keep walking the way you actually want to go, and eventually the ground will admit it.
